results.key_finding: Migraine is a frequent source of non-specific white matter lesions and of MS misdiagnosis. Small punctate subcortical foci are non-specific; ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions are typical of MS.

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. Migraine-related white matter lesions are typically small and subcortical and do not involve the spinal cord.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not attribute the lesions to migraine or the symptoms to anxiety: ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical, pontine, enhancing and spinal cord lesions are not migraine-related
Do not reject the diagnosis because the CSF oligoclonal bands are negative
Do not give high-dose corticosteroids now: the examination shows no new deficit affecting function and the unsteadiness episode has resolved
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord: 4 of 5, so DIT is not required), and explain that negative CSF oligoclonal bands do not exclude MS.
Revise the earlier attribution of the white matter lesions to migraine and explain the diagnosis to the patient.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (lesions in four regions, an enhancing periventricular lesion, a symptomatic cervical cord lesion), through shared decision-making.

Before an anti-CD20 antibody or S1P modulator, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), update vaccinations and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before the first dose.
Replace vitamin D (25-OH vitamin D 21 ng/mL).

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, altered awareness or episodic confusion: EEG does not inform the episodic vertigo or sensory symptoms.
CT does not show demyelinating lesions; the question is answered only by MRI.
No cardiac symptom, murmur or embolic pattern: echocardiography does not address the white matter lesions.
Positional vertigo lasting seconds without syncope or palpitations: cardiac monitoring adds nothing.
FDG-PET does not distinguish demyelinating from migraine-related lesions and has no role in this work-up.

differential.key_features: Supports: migraine since 19 and three small subcortical foci. Against: ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, a juxtacortical and a pontine lesion, an enhancing lesion and a dorsal C5-C6 cord lesion, none of which migraine produces.
No optic neuritis, area postrema syndrome or longitudinally extensive myelitis; the cord lesion is short and dorsal and the brain lesions are ovoid periventricular and juxtacortical.
No optic neuritis, ADEM-like encephalopathy or conus lesion; small discrete lesions rather than fluffy confluent ones.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jianjun Liu is a 22-year-old right-handed graduate student who was admitted for further workup after presenting to the outpatient neurology clinic with a six-month history of episodic vertigo, progressive fatigue, and intermittent tingling in his left hand. His symptoms began approximately six months ago when he first noticed brief episodes of room-spinning vertigo lasting 30 to 60 seconds, occurring two to three times per week, often triggered by quick head movements or standing up rapidly. He was initially evaluated by his primary care physician who diagnosed benign positional vertigo and prescribed meclizine, which provided minimal relief. Over the subsequent months, he developed a persistent sense of fatigue that he describes as unlike anything he has experienced before, not relieved by rest, and significantly impacting his ability to concentrate on his graduate coursework. He has also noticed intermittent tingling and a sensation of pins and needles in his left hand and fingers, occurring unpredictably, sometimes lasting minutes and occasionally persisting for several hours before resolving spontaneously. He reports that these sensory episodes do not follow a dermatomal pattern and are not associated with hand weakness or clumsiness. Approximately two months ago, he experienced a two-week period during which he felt unsteady on his feet, particularly when walking in dimly lit environments, but this resolved completely without intervention. He attributes much of his symptomatology to stress and sleep deprivation related to his thesis work. His primary care physician obtained a brain MRI after his most recent visit due to persistent symptoms, which was interpreted as showing several small non-specific white matter lesions, thought to be consistent with migraine-related changes given his history. He was referred to neurology for further evaluation and was admitted for a more comprehensive diagnostic workup including lumbar puncture. He denies any history of optic neuritis, limb weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, heat sensitivity, or electric shock-like sensations with neck flexion. He has had no recent fevers, weight loss, joint pain, oral ulcers, or skin rashes.
